title: The 'Dionysus-Osiris' self-presentation in the East
description: Antony cultivated an association with the god Dionysus in his eastern territories, presenting himself as the New Dionysus. In Egypt, this was syncretized with Osiris, with Cleopatra as Isis-Aphrodite. This divine self-presentation was exploited by Octavian's propaganda to portray Antony as an eastern despot who had abandoned Roman values.

title: Shakespeare's 'Antony and Cleopatra' as reception
description: William Shakespeare's tragedy 'Antony and Cleopatra' (c. 1607) is the most influential modern reception of Antony. Shakespeare follows Plutarch's narrative closely (via Thomas North's 1579 translation) but transforms Antony into a tragic hero torn between Roman duty and Egyptian passion. This literary character is a reception, not a historical document.

title: The 'dissolute youth' tradition
description: Cicero (Phil. 2.44-46), Plutarch (Ant. 2-4), and other sources describe Antony's youth as marked by heavy drinking, womanizing, and debt. Plutarch claims Antony was 'enslaved' to the courtesan Cytheris. This tradition may have been exaggerated by Cicero's hostile rhetoric and later Augustan propaganda to contrast the 'debauched' Antony with the 'virtuous' Octavian.

title: Augustan propaganda: the 'Roman traitor' narrative
description: The image of Antony as a Roman who abandoned his country for a foreign queen (Cleopatra) is a product of Octavian's propaganda campaign (the 'inimici' tradition). Key elements include: the Donations of Alexandria as treason, the will as proof of Egyptian loyalty, and the Battle of Actium as a defense of Rome against the East. This narrative was perpetuated by Augustan poets (Horace, Virgil) and pervades the surviving ancient sources.

title: Not a Roman emperor — clarification
description: Antony was never a Roman emperor. He was a triumvir (43-33 BCE), consul (44 BCE, 34 BCE), and a leading general of the late Republic. His defeat and death enabled Octavian's sole rule and the establishment of the Principate (27 BCE), but Antony himself died before the imperial system was formally established. Any reference to Antony as 'emperor' is historically incorrect.
